articles.title: NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat
articles.summary: The four crew members in NASA’s simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation in a confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.
articles.content:
Members of NASA’s CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog) Mission 2 crew stands in their workspace after spending a year in their isolated and confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. (from left: James Spicer, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis, and Ross Elder). NASA

The four crew members in NASA’s simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation in a confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. For the past 365 days, the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew members have operated as though they were on the Red Planet, growing crops, managing limited resources, navigating communication delays, and conducting suited extravehicular activities on a simulated Martian surface.

Crew members include Ross Elder, mission commander; Ellen Ellis, medical officer; Matthew Montgomery, science officer; and James Spicer, flight engineer. They entered their 1,700 square foot 3D-printed habitat Oct. 19, 2025. Leading up to the one-year mark of their 378‑day mission, science teams at NASA prepared to process health and performance data collected on the crew. This critical data can help NASA balance priorities and develop methods that counter spaceflight risks during future long-duration missions on Mars.

“We are extremely proud of the crew for their commitment and achievements over the last year on such a fast-paced, highly demanding mission,” said Grace Douglas, CHAPEA principal investigator. “The entire CHAPEA team is excited to congratulate the crew in person.”

The crew will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, to conclude their mission. They will have a chance to reconnect with their families, who they’ve only spoken with via email over the course of their mission with a Mars-like communication delay. The crew will then begin two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefs with NASA scientists.

These debriefs and evaluations will help scientists learn what it takes for crews to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions, giving NASA insight into what future explorers may need to stay healthy, productive, and connected during missions far from Earth.

For example, data could shed light on how limited food and exercise systems will influence NASA’s ability to achieve mission objectives, including spacewalks on the surface of Mars. Some data also could help NASA foster autonomy and build decision-making support systems that best aid crew with communication delays lasting up to 45 minutes each way.

“This mission has been incredibly valuable in starting to teach us how to understand requirements for year-long missions, including medical and psychological care, via communication delays,” said Michael Stenger, chief scientist for NASA’s Human Research Program. “When combining this Mars-realistic mission analog with a suite of physiological, psychological, and performance measures in a rigorously controlled environment, we’ll be able to translate the knowledge from these experiences to Moon Base and beyond.”

To watch the CHAPEA Mission 2 egress ceremony on Oct. 31, visit:

https://www.youtube.com/live/2MONMgAmXNU

James Spicer, Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 flight engineer, participates in an extravehicular geological activity. NASA Ellen Ellis, CHAPEA Mission 2 medical officer, performs a medical task with Ross Elder, mission commander. NASA The CHAPEA crew showcases the instruments they brought on their mission. The crew elected to include instruments as part of their personal item allowance. From left: James Spicer, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery, and Ross Elder. NASA CHAPEA Mission 2 crew members Ellen Ellis (left) and Ross Elder (right) conduct a maintenance task during a simulated extravehicular activity, also known as a spacewalk. NASA Photos that the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew arranged around a boot print in the simulated Martian sand outside their habitat. NASA

____

NASA’s Human Research Program

NASA’s Human Research Program pursues methods and technologies to support safe, productive human space travel. Through science conducted in laboratories, ground-based analogs, commercial missions, the International Space Station and Artemis missions, the program scrutinizes how spaceflight affects human bodies and behaviors. Such research drives the program’s quest to innovate ways that keep astronauts healthy and mission ready as human space exploration expands to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

articles.personality_title: NASA crew completes one-year Mars simulation to prepare for future space missions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is preparing for future missions to Mars by simulating what it would be like to live and work on the Red Planet. This helps scientists understand the challenges astronauts might face during long trips far from Earth.

**What happened** – Four crew members spent a full year living inside a small, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. From October 2025 to October 2026, they acted as if they were on Mars. They grew crops, managed limited supplies, dealt with communication delays like those on Mars, and practiced spacewalks on a fake Martian surface. The crew included a mission commander, medical officer, science officer, and flight engineer.

**Impact** – This mission is important because it gave NASA detailed information about how people handle living alone in small spaces for a long time, how their health and mood change, and how they manage tasks with delays in communication. These insights will help NASA design better support for astronauts on real Mars missions, including medical care and decision-making tools.

**What's next step** – The crew will leave their habitat on October 31, 2026, and begin two weeks of tests and interviews with NASA scientists. Researchers will study the data collected during the mission to improve future space travel, including missions to the Moon and Mars. NASA will also share the mission’s end ceremony online for the public to watch.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s one-year Mars simulation has provided key knowledge about living and working on Mars, helping prepare astronauts for future long space journeys.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’équipage de la NASA achève une simulation d’un an sur Mars pour préparer les futures missions spatiales
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La NASA prépare les futures missions vers Mars en simulant la vie et le travail sur la planète rouge. Cela aide les scientifiques à comprendre les défis auxquels les astronautes pourraient faire face lors de longs voyages loin de la Terre.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Quatre membres d’équipage ont passé une année entière à vivre dans un petit habitat imprimé en 3D au centre spatial Johnson de la NASA à Houston. D’octobre 2025 à octobre 2026, ils ont agi comme s’ils étaient sur Mars. Ils ont cultivé des plantes, géré des ressources limitées, fait face à des retards de communication similaires à ceux de Mars, et pratiqué des sorties dans l’espace sur une surface martienne simulée. L’équipage comprenait un commandant de mission, un médecin, un scientifique et un ingénieur de vol.

**Impact** – Cette mission est importante car elle a fourni à la NASA des informations détaillées sur la manière dont les personnes vivent dans de petits espaces isolés pendant longtemps, comment leur santé et leur humeur évoluent, et comment elles gèrent les tâches avec des retards de communication. Ces connaissances aideront la NASA à mieux soutenir les astronautes lors des vraies missions martiennes, notamment pour les soins médicaux et la prise de décision.

**Prochaines étapes** – L’équipage quittera son habitat le 31 octobre 2026 et commencera deux semaines d’évaluations et d’entretiens avec les scientifiques de la NASA. Les chercheurs étudieront les données recueillies pendant la mission pour améliorer les futurs voyages spatiaux, y compris les missions vers la Lune et Mars. La NASA diffusera également en ligne la cérémonie de fin de mission.

**En une phrase** – La simulation d’un an sur Mars par la NASA a apporté des connaissances clés sur la vie et le travail sur Mars, aidant à préparer les astronautes pour de longs voyages spatiaux futurs.
articles.personality_title_es: La tripulación de la NASA completa una simulación de un año en Marte para preparar futuras misiones espaciales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La NASA se prepara para futuras misiones a Marte simulando cómo sería vivir y trabajar en el Planeta Rojo. Esto ayuda a los científicos a entender los desafíos que enfrentarán los astronautas en viajes largos lejos de la Tierra.

**Qué pasó** – Cuatro miembros de la tripulación pasaron un año completo viviendo dentro de un pequeño hábitat impreso en 3D en el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA en Houston. Desde octubre de 2025 hasta octubre de 2026, actuaron como si estuvieran en Marte. Cultivaron plantas, administraron recursos limitados, enfrentaron retrasos en la comunicación similares a los de Marte y practicaron caminatas espaciales en una superficie marciana simulada. La tripulación incluía un comandante de misión, un oficial médico, un oficial científico y un ingeniero de vuelo.

**Impacto** – Esta misión es importante porque proporcionó a la NASA información detallada sobre cómo las personas manejan vivir solas en espacios pequeños durante mucho tiempo, cómo cambia su salud y estado de ánimo, y cómo realizan tareas con retrasos en la comunicación. Estos datos ayudarán a la NASA a diseñar mejor el apoyo para los astronautas en misiones reales a Marte, incluyendo atención médica y herramientas para la toma de decisiones.

**Próximo paso** – La tripulación saldrá de su hábitat el 31 de octubre de 2026 y comenzará dos semanas de pruebas y entrevistas con científicos de la NASA. Los investigadores estudiarán los datos recolectados durante la misión para mejorar los viajes espaciales futuros, incluyendo misiones a la Luna y Marte. La NASA también compartirá la ceremonia de fin de misión en línea para que el público la vea.

**Frase clave** – La simulación de un año en Marte de la NASA proporcionó conocimientos clave sobre vivir y trabajar en Marte, ayudando a preparar a los astronautas para futuros viajes espaciales largos.
